extractedReferences.rawText:  There is an overlap of responsibility between the Railway Undertaking and the Infrastructure Manager: for a given value of the braked weight percentage, the shape of the EBD curve is “imposed” by the IM regardless of the architecture and performance of the rolling stock braking system. As a result the (not quantified) reliability of the EBD curve may vary from one train type to another one and the integrated correction factors may have to be aligned to the less performing train in terms of dispersion and resilience to wet conditions.

extractedReferences.rawText: For conventional passenger trains, the Railway Undertaking has the full freedom to opt for the preconfigured emergency deceleration profile and rolling stock correction factors or for the capture of the braked weight percentage and its associated conversion. ETCS even offers the possibility for the train preparer/driver, if the ETCS on-board is so configured, to select one or the other method, this feature being useful for locomotives that alternatively pull passenger trains and freight trains.

extractedReferences.rawText: Today, almost all the conventional lines are fitted with optical signals. Even on those lines fitted with an underlying legacy CCS system, the driving of the trains is primarily based on the observance by the driver of the optical signal aspects. The warning signal requires the driver to start braking in due time when the train must be brought to a stop from the nominal line speed.

referenceData.citation: Today, almost all the conventional lines are fitted with optical signals. Even on those lines fitted with an underlying legacy CCS system, the driving of the trains is primarily based on the observance by the driver of the optical signal aspects. The warning signal requires the driver to start braking in due time when the train must be brought to a stop from the nominal line speed.

extractedReferences.rawText: These signals are therefore located in order to match the braking performance of the preferred type of rolling stock operating on the concerned line, taking into account the slopes and possibly some safety margins.

referenceData.citation: These signals are therefore located in order to match the braking performance of the preferred type of rolling stock operating on the concerned line, taking into account the slopes and possibly some safety margins.

extractedReferences.rawText: When trains with less good braking performance (e.g. freight trains) have to operate on a line designed for better trains, the driver is instructed (generally through its driver’s route book or eventually through the legacy CCS system) to run at a lower speed than the nominal line speed, keeping in mind that the location from which he starts to brake (the warning signal) remains the same for all trains.

referenceData.citation: When trains with less good braking performance (e.g. freight trains) have to operate on a line designed for better trains, the driver is instructed (generally through its driver’s route book or eventually through the legacy CCS system) to run at a lower speed than the nominal line speed, keeping in mind that the location from which he starts to brake (the warning signal) remains the same for all trains.

extractedReferences.rawText: In a few words, driving with optical signals implies that the location where to start braking is fixed, while the initial speed is adapted in order to match the braking performance of the train. With ETCS, this is exactly the contrary: the initial speed is constant, while the location where to start braking is adapted according to the braking performance of the train.

referenceData.citation: In a few words, driving with optical signals implies that the location where to start braking is fixed, while the initial speed is adapted in order to match the braking performance of the train. With ETCS, this is exactly the contrary: the initial speed is constant, while the location where to start braking is adapted according to the braking performance of the train.

extractedReferences.rawText: When operating trains under the ETCS full supervision, the Indication distance at line speed (i.e. the distance from the Indication supervision limit at line speed to the stop location) is called the perturbation distance and is a major contributor to the headway that can be achieved on a line. The headway is generally expressed as the time between two consecutive trains, but can also be represented by the minimum distance between trains that allows them to safely run at the desired line speed, without being disrupted.

referenceData.citation: When operating trains under the ETCS full supervision, the Indication distance at line speed (i.e. the distance from the Indication supervision limit at line speed to the stop location) is called the perturbation distance and is a major contributor to the headway that can be achieved on a line. The headway is generally expressed as the time between two consecutive trains, but can also be represented by the minimum distance between trains that allows them to safely run at the desired line speed, without being disrupted.
